faq.q: Can foreigners buy property in Greece?
faq.a: Yes. EU and non-EU citizens can buy property in Greece. You need a Greek tax number (AFM), a Greek bank account and, in practice, an independent lawyer. In some border areas, non-EU buyers need a permit before the purchase, and your lawyer checks this for each property. Rules are stated as of November 2026.

faq.q: What are the costs and taxes of buying property in Greece?
faq.a: As of November 2026: transfer tax of 3.09% on a resale (3% plus a municipal surcharge), while VAT on new builds is suspended until 31/12/2026. Lawyer, notary and land-registry costs vary and typically add several percent in total. After the purchase you pay the annual ENFIA property tax. Our lawyer confirms the figures for each case.

faq.q: What are the pitfalls of buying property in Greece?
faq.a: The main ones are unpermitted extensions, mismatches between the title, the plot and the cadastre, debts on the property, unclear buildability of land outside the town plan, and co-owners who have not all agreed to sell. An independent lawyer and an engineer who check everything before you sign are the best protection.

faq.q: Can UK or US citizens buy property in Greece after Brexit?
faq.a: Yes. UK and US citizens can buy property in Greece as non-EU citizens, with a Greek tax number, a bank account and a lawyer. Border-area permits may apply in some places. Owning property does not give residence: to stay beyond the Schengen limit of 90 days in any 180, you need a residence permit such as the Golden Visa.

faq.q: Do I need a Greek lawyer and tax number to buy property?
faq.a: You need a Greek tax number (AFM) for any purchase. You should also hire an independent Greek lawyer, who checks the title, permits and debts, represents you at the notary and can obtain your tax number with a power of attorney. Your lawyer confirms what applies in your case.

intro: Buying property in Greece as a foreigner is straightforward once you know the steps: get a Greek tax number, open a bank account, hire an independent lawyer, check the property, then sign at the notary. This guide explains each stage, the costs and taxes as of November 2026, and the pitfalls to avoid. We are an agency in Halkidiki, Northern Greece, so we finish with local tips. All figures are to be confirmed by our lawyer, and this guide is general information, not legal advice.
body:
Can foreigners buy property in Greece?

Yes. Greek law allows foreigners to buy property, and most purchases by foreigners need no special approval. EU citizens buy on the same terms as Greek citizens. Citizens of non-EU countries, including the UK and the USA, can also buy.

The main exception concerns certain border areas of Greece, where buyers from outside the EU need a permit before the purchase. Whether a property falls in such an area is something your lawyer checks for each case.

Every buyer needs two things, as of November 2026:

  • a Greek tax number (AFM), which your lawyer can often obtain for you with a power of attorney
  • a Greek bank account, through which the purchase price is paid so that the money is documented

You do not have to be in Greece for most steps. With a power of attorney, your lawyer can apply for your tax number, deal with the bank and even sign the final deed for you.

Buying a property does not by itself give you the right to live in Greece. Non-EU citizens who want residence can look at the Golden Visa, explained on our separate page.

Step by step: from viewing to the notary

The usual path looks like this:

  • Search and viewings. Shortlist homes online, then view them in person or by video.
  • Tax number and bank account. Get your AFM and open a Greek bank account.
  • Independent lawyer. Your lawyer represents you, not the seller or the agent.
  • Due diligence. The lawyer checks the title at the land registry or cadastre, plus any debts or mortgages; an engineer checks the building permit and any unpermitted spaces.
  • Offer and preliminary contract. Once price and terms are agreed, a preliminary contract with a deposit may be signed, setting the conditions for completion.
  • Transfer tax. The tax is paid before the final deed.
  • Final contract at the notary. Buyer and seller, or their representatives, sign the deed before a notary.
  • Registration. The deed is registered at the land registry or cadastre, which completes the transfer.

The notary is a public official who drafts the deed and checks that the required certificates are present. That does not replace your own lawyer's checks. The whole process can take from a few weeks to a few months, depending mainly on how quickly the documents are ready.

Most foreign buyers pay from their own funds, as a Greek mortgage can be hard to get for non-residents. If you need financing, talk to banks early, in Greece and in your home country, so the loan does not hold up the contract.

Plan your viewing trip well. Send us your budget, preferred areas and must-haves in advance, and we prepare a shortlist so that you see the right homes in a few days. Video viewings help you narrow the list before you travel.

Costs and taxes when buying (as of November 2026)

All figures below are as of November 2026 and are to be confirmed by our lawyer for your case.

  • Transfer tax: 3.09% on resale property (3% plus a municipal surcharge).
  • VAT on new builds: new buildings are normally subject to VAT instead of transfer tax, but VAT is suspended until 31/12/2026.
  • Lawyer, notary and land registry: these vary with the price and the work involved; together they typically come to several percent of the price.
  • Engineer: a fee for checking the legal status of the building and, where needed, legalising small deviations.
  • Agency fee: agree it in writing with your agent before you start.

Ask for a written estimate of all costs before you make an offer, so you know your total budget and not just the price.

The transfer tax is calculated on the price in the contract, which cannot be lower than the official tax value set by the state for that property. Make sure the full price you pay appears in the deed and is paid through a bank, so the money is traceable if you sell later.

Pitfalls to avoid: permits, legalisation and debts

Most problems come from skipped checks. The common ones are:

  • Unpermitted building. Extra rooms, closed-in balconies or basements built without a permit. Many can be legalised, but this costs money and must be settled before the sale.
  • Title and boundaries. The plot on the ground must match the title and the cadastre. Mismatches can delay or block the sale.
  • Debts and mortgages. Loans, seizures or unpaid taxes on the property must be cleared before completion.
  • Land outside the town plan. Buildability depends on zoning, plot size and road access; a seller's promise is not enough.
  • Several owners. Inherited properties often have co-owners, and every one of them must sign.
  • Missing certificates. An energy certificate and a certificate from an engineer on the legal status of the building are needed at the notary; get them early.
  • Letting plans. If you plan holiday lets, check the local rules and registration before you buy, not after.
  • Payments outside the contract. Always pay the full price by bank transfer, as recorded in the deed.

An independent lawyer and an engineer working for you, not for the seller, are the best protection.

Buying from the UK or USA

Since Brexit, UK citizens buy as non-EU citizens. In practice this changes little for the purchase itself: you need the same tax number, bank account and lawyer, and border-area rules may apply. The same is true for US citizens.

What changes is residence. Non-EU owners can usually stay in the Schengen area for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. To stay longer, you need a residence permit, such as the Golden Visa or a permit for people with sufficient independent income. Your lawyer can explain which route fits you.

Many buyers from the UK and the USA complete the purchase remotely by giving a power of attorney to their lawyer, signed at a Greek consulate or certified with an apostille. They visit to view the shortlist and come back when the keys are ready.

Annual costs: ENFIA property tax and running costs

Owning property in Greece brings yearly costs. As of November 2026, to be confirmed by our lawyer:

  • ENFIA: the annual property tax, based on the official value, size and location of the property
  • Utilities: electricity, water and internet, plus municipal charges that are often included in the electricity bill
  • Common charges in shared buildings or complexes
  • Insurance, which we recommend for every home
  • Tax on rental income, if you let the property
  • Maintenance of the garden, pool and building

If you are away for most of the year, property management can handle keys, cleaning, repairs and bills. We offer this after the purchase.

If you let your home to holiday guests, the property must be registered for short-term letting and the income declared in Greece. Speak to an accountant before you start, as the rules on tax and registration are updated from time to time.

Rental income is taxed separately from your other income, on a scale that starts at 15% and rises with the amount. A private pool adds a yearly luxury-living tax charged per square metre of pool, and raises the minimum income the tax office presumes you have. The rates change with the annual budget, so your accountant confirms the current ones.

Buying in Halkidiki: local tips

The start of the Kassandra peninsula is about an hour by car from Thessaloniki airport, so short viewing trips are easy. Some tips from working only in this region:

  • View in more than one area. Kassandra, Sithonia, Nea Propontida, Aristotelis and Polygyros feel very different.
  • Visit out of season if you plan to stay beyond summer, as some resort villages are very quiet in winter.
  • Check the road access to the home, especially for plots and hillside houses.
  • Ask how far the nearest year-round shop, pharmacy and health centre are.
  • Think about who will look after the home when you leave; gardens and pools need care through the summer.
  • Compare first-line homes with homes a few streets back; the price difference can be large, while the walk to the beach is often short.
  • For the Golden Visa, as of November 2026 Halkidiki is in the €400,000 zone for one residential property of at least 120 m².

When you are ready, browse our listings and book a viewing in person or by video.
